title: Gift Card Scammers Target PIN Numbers
description: The Retail Gift Card Association says it now recommends retailers use packaging which "covers and protects magnetic strips and gift card PINs.

asr.full_text: This is where many of us pick the perfect present. And I learned the hard way, this is also where criminals like to lurk. I sent my dad a gift card to Outback Steakhouse for Father's Day. But when he tried to use it at this restaurant in California, the manager said the card had a zero balance. So we tracked the package and the card activity and learned while the gift card was being shipped to my dad,. Someone else was already using it at an Outback in Dallas to buy drinks and appetizers. The Dallas location told us the customer had the card number and PIN and both had been keyed in,. A common practice when a customer does not have the card in hand. How did they get my card and PIN number? Some of them will just do really old school way. They'll go into the establishment, they'll start writing down numbers. Attorneys with the Federal Trade Commission say this is called gift card draining. We searched several stores and found while some cards hide the numbers and pins, others are easy to see. You can see the pin on every one. Some require a scratch off. Scratch here for CID. Or have a silver zebra-like sticker covering the pin. So the next question is, how do the thieves know when the cards have money? Some of them, again, depending on the level of sophistication, will just go online, do it by hand. Others have developed custom written software. That software will then return the result to the hacker and say,. Here are the card numbers that have been activated and here's the money that you can now use. Outback tells us we changed the way we produced gift cards last year to cover the PIN number. However, older cards may still be found on shelves. Of course, if this happens, we fully reimburse our customers. That includes my dad, who can now enjoy my gift. Ginger Allen for CBS News, Dallas.

textual.observation: The report describes gift-card draining in which a person obtains a gift-card number and PIN and uses the card before the intended recipient, resulting in a zero balance.

evidence.quote: Someone else was already using it at an Outback in Dallas to buy drinks and appetizers.
The Dallas location told us the customer had the card number and PIN and both had been keyed in,
Attorneys with the Federal Trade Commission say this is called gift card draining.

textual.context: Presented as a news report about a customer's experience and a described fraud mechanism, with attribution to the Federal Trade Commission.
textual.potential_relevance: The source links access to a card number and PIN with use of stored value before the recipient can use the gift card.
textual.limitations: These records do not establish the identity or intent of the person who used the card, how the number and PIN were obtained in this particular case, or any broader prevalence.

textual.observation: The report describes custom-written software being used to identify activated gift-card numbers and the available money.

evidence.quote: Others have developed custom written software.
That software will then return the result to the hacker and say,
Here are the card numbers that have been activated and here's the money that you can now use.

textual.context: Presented as a reported explanation of how some people detect when gift cards have been activated; the passage does not instruct the audience to use the software.
textual.potential_relevance: The source connects software output identifying activated cards and balances with subsequent access to gift-card funds.
textual.limitations: The records do not provide the software, show its operation, establish who created or used it, or establish that any particular viewer could access it.

visual.observation: An Outback Steakhouse gift card is shown with overlaid text reading "$0 balance" in front of an Outback restaurant exterior.
visual.context: Appears in a report-style visual sequence about gift cards; no direct viewer instruction is visible in this frame.
visual.potential_relevance: The observed stored-value balance claim is linked in nearby sampled frames to gift-card packaging and PIN/security-code visuals, which may be relevant to reviewing a described gift-card value-loss mechanism.
visual.limitations: The sampled frames do not establish how the balance became zero, whether any transaction occurred, or whether the card was valid or used.

visual.observation: Close-up gift card images show barcodes, visible number strings, and a labeled PIN/security-code area, including one frame with an arrow pointing at a scratch-off style panel.
visual.context: The visuals appear demonstrative or explanatory rather than a direct request for viewers to use the codes.
visual.potential_relevance: The frames show gift-card identifiers and PIN/security areas in the same sequence as a zero-balance card and brand statement about covering PIN numbers, forming a concrete visual relationship for potential review of gift-card credential exposure.
visual.limitations: The frames do not show a complete readable card credential set being used, do not prove any code was copied, and do not establish intent or outcome.

visual.observation: A quoted on-screen statement beside the Outback logo says, "...we changed the way we produce gift cards last year to cover the pin number. However, older cards may still be found".
visual.context: Presented as a brand-related quotation in an explanatory segment; the source of the quote is not independently verified within the sampled frames.
visual.potential_relevance: The visible statement links a brand production change to PIN coverage and older-card availability, which conditionally relates to the preceding visuals of exposed PIN/security-code areas.
visual.limitations: The frames cannot verify the quote's source, completeness, date, or whether any specific card shown is affected.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents a report about alleged gift-card draining, including reported zero balances, PIN exposure, and prior unauthorized use. The discussion of software and keyboard activity explains the reported mechanism and is not presented as an audience instruction or promotion. PIN-protection changes and possible reimbursement provide consumer-protection and retailer-response context.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The central content examines reported unauthorized gift-card use, describes how card identifiers may be exposed, and reports a retailer response.
